desc:
A subtree consists of a node together with all of its descendants. It is height-balanced if at every node inside it the heights of the left and right sub-subtrees differ by at most 1 (an empty side has height 0; height counts nodes on the longest downward path).

Return the number of nodes in the largest height-balanced subtree of the tree. The empty tree gives 0; a single node is always balanced.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, -1, -1, 4, 4] the whole tree is not balanced, but the subtree rooted at the left child (the nodes 2, 3, 3, 4, 4) is, so the answer is 5.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Checking every node as a candidate root and testing balance from scratch is easy but quadratic on skewed trees.
A subtree is balanced only if both child subtrees are balanced and their heights differ by at most 1. So a node can decide using what its children already know.
From last node to first, store for each node: its height, its size, and whether it is balanced. The answer is the largest size among balanced nodes.
editorial: Define for each node three facts about its subtree: height, size and balanced. A node is balanced when both children are balanced (a missing child counts as balanced with height 0) and their heights differ by at most 1. Its size is 1 + size(left) + size(right) and its height is 1 + max(...).

All three facts depend only on the children, so one backward pass through the level-order array computes them. Track the maximum size over balanced nodes. Time and space are linear, versus O(n<sup>2</sup>) for retesting each subtree independently.
